## The headline workflow

```{r}
library(magic.table)
library(googlesheets4)

ss <- gs4_create("Q1 sales analysis")

write_analytical_table(
  ss,
  sales_q1,
  sheet     = "Sales",
  title     = "Q1 Sales by Region",
  summaries = c(Total = "SUM", Average = "AVERAGE")
)
```

The resulting sheet:

| Row | Content                              |
| --- | ------------------------------------ |
| 1   | Title row                            |
| 2   | (blank)                              |
| 3   | Column headers                       |
| 4–N | Data                                 |
| N+1 | First summary row                    |
| N+2 | Second summary row                   |

## Restricting which columns get summarized

By default, summaries apply to every numeric column. Pass `cols` to restrict:

```{r}
write_analytical_table(
  ss,
  sales_q1,
  sheet     = "Sales",
  title     = "Q1 Sales by Region",
  summaries = c(Total = "SUM"),
  cols      = c("revenue", "units")
)
```

## Composing your own layouts

For non-standard layouts, drop down a level. `make_summary_row()` returns a
one-row tibble whose numeric columns are `gs4_formula()`-wrapped strings — ready
for `googlesheets4::sheet_append()`.

```{r}
sheet_write(sales_q1, ss, sheet = "Sales")

totals <- make_summary_row(
  sales_q1,
  data_start_row = 2,
  label          = "Total",
  fn             = "SUM"
)

sheet_append(ss, totals, sheet = "Sales")
```

`col_letter()` converts a 1-based column index to its A1 letter
(`col_letter(28)` returns `"AB"`) if you need to assemble formulas by hand.

## The magic.table: recorded-computation tables

The helpers above compute summaries eagerly in R. A `magic.table` goes further:
it wraps a data frame so that `dplyr::mutate()` *records* each expression as
column provenance instead of computing it. Those recorded computations are then
**exported as live formulas** to an external table — Google Sheets today (other
backends, and reconciling external edits, are on the roadmap). Editing a source
cell in Sheets recomputes the derived columns, because they are real formulas,
not pasted values.

```{r magic-table}
library(magic.table)
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble::tibble(
  region = c("E", "W", "S"),
  sales  = c(120, 80, 60),
  cost   = c( 40, 30, 20)
)

df |>
  magic.table() |>
  mutate(margin     = sales - cost,
         margin_pct = margin / sales) |>
  write_sheet(ss, sheet = "Sales", start_row = 3)
```

The `margin` column ends up holding `=(B4)-(C4)`, `=(B5)-(C5)`, … and
`margin_pct` holds `=(D4)/(B4)`, … .

### Inspecting column provenance

A `magic.table` remembers how each column came to be. `provenance()` reports,
per column, whether it is an original `source` column or one `computed` by a
recorded `mutate()`, and the expression that defines it — derived on demand, no
auth needed:

```{r provenance, eval = TRUE}
library(magic.table)
library(dplyr)

tibble::tibble(sales = c(120, 80), cost = c(40, 30)) |>
  magic.table() |>
  mutate(margin = sales - cost,
         margin_pct = margin / sales) |>
  provenance()
```

### Previewing without auth

`as_sheet_cells()` returns exactly what `write_sheet()` *would* push, without
contacting Google — handy for sanity-checking formulas (and the testability
lever for the whole package):

```{r preview, eval = TRUE}
library(magic.table)
library(dplyr)

tibble::tibble(sales = c(120, 80), cost = c(40, 30)) |>
  magic.table() |>
  mutate(margin = sales - cost,
         margin_pct = margin / sales) |>
  as_sheet_cells(start_row = 3)
```

### Extending the translator

The default dialect covers arithmetic, comparisons, logical operators,
`ifelse`, and a small set of math/predicate functions (`abs`, `round`,
`sqrt`, `pmin`, `pmax`, `is.na`). Anything else errors with a hint pointing
at `register_sheet_translator()`:

```{r register}
register_sheet_translator("paste0", function(args, ctx) {
  paste(args, collapse = "&")
})
```

### Syncing and no-clobber reconciliation

`write_sheet()` returns the `magic.table` with a **bound backend** — the
connection (`ss` / `sheet` / `start_row`) plus a snapshot of what was written.
Capture it to keep that connection:

```{r sync, eval = FALSE}
mt <- df |>
  magic.table() |>
  mutate(margin = sales - cost) |>
  write_sheet(ss, sheet = "Sales", start_row = 3)
```

On a re-write to the same target, magic.table first polls the sheet and compares
it against that snapshot. If someone edited the sheet in the meantime, the write
is **refused with a warning** rather than silently clobbering their edit:

```{r reconcile, eval = FALSE}
mt <- write_sheet(mt, ss, sheet = "Sales", start_row = 3)
#> Warning: The target sheet has changed since magic.table last wrote it;
#> not overwriting. Pass `overwrite = TRUE` to write anyway.

# write anyway:
mt <- write_sheet(mt, ss, sheet = "Sales", start_row = 3, overwrite = TRUE)
```
